utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those listening and watching the procedures. Before the witness will be brought in, I would like to raise one matter. The Chamber has received the Prosecution's notification regarding remaining witnesses, filed today, on the 5th of July, 2011, in which the Prosecution submits, I quote, "a breakdown of its remaining 18 witnesses." The Chamber has reviewed all witnesses the Prosecution had previously indicated in its 65 ter list, and has identified six remaining witnesses for which it invites the Prosecution to clarify their status. The Chamber would like to ask the Prosecution to confirm that the two following witnesses have been withdrawn as well. These are Witness Number 16, Johan de Koeijer, as well as Witness Michael Hedley, who was subject to the Chamber's decision of the 31st of August, 2010. Further, with regard to the remaining four witnesses which are also mentioned in footnote 2 of the Prosecution's notification of yesterday, filed today, and were subject of the Chamber's decision of 7th of July, 2010, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to clarify its intention in relation to the 65 ter numbers 63, 67, 72, and 80. Is the Prosecution in a position to clarify these matters now, or if not, at which stage? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. I can get back to you after the next break, and I'm sure to clarify this for you, so that should be no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it that there are no other matters to be discussed. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday still applies. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Please, if there is any reason for a break, please let the Chamber know. Then we will have a break because of your medical situation. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation. Is your microphone switched on? Please try again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, the interpreters don't hear you. There is a technical problem with the microphone. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Tolimir's microphone is on. There must be something else, some other technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have now changed my microphone. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the interpreters could hear you. If it is possible for you to use the other microphone, that would be very helpful. Just start your cross-examination, and we will see how it works.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we need a technician to help us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still not receiving interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'll try it again. Do you receive now an interpretation of what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I am receiving interpretation. It was my mistake. When I switched microphones, I did not switch channels at the same time, so that was due to my mistake. I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No problem at all. This was still in relation to Monday. Now we start with Tuesday. Mr. Tolimir, please proceed and continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wish the witness good health, a speedy recovery, and fast return home. Yesterday, we left it off with the rules, and we're going to look at another provision from the Rules of Service of the Security Services. Can we look at D02 -- D203, because I have some more questions to ask you before I round the topic off. I would kindly ask the electronic courtroom to display D203. We can see it now. This is Rules of Service of Security Organs in the Armed Forces. Can we have pages 10 and 9 in English and Serbian respectively. Now we have the English version. I'm interested in Article 16, and we have it in the Serbian as well. It says here: "The security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment, and it is responsible to that officer for its work ..." My question: When it comes to the Rules of Service, do they regulate who the security organs are subordinated in a unit, and what was the situation like in your unit? Who was the security organ in your unit subordinated to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that I had not studied the rules and that I'm not familiar with the text of the rules. It is very difficult for me to say anything or to share with you my opinions about the rules. Since I am not familiar with these provisions, since I'm not familiar with the rules governing the work of the security organs, I don't know what to say. I can only read the text, but I'm not familiar with it. I was never aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The fact that you were not familiar with the rules, which is only normal - I'm not familiar with your rules - was that the reason why you provided answers which differ from what is provided for by the rules? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to answer questions to the best of my recollection and to the best of my knowledge, and that's what I did. I said what I had known at the time. That's what I was asked to do, and that's how I answered. That was the only way I could answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, could you please tell us who the security organ in your unit was subordinated to? I'm asking for your answer based on what you know from practice.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what it says here, the security organ should be subordinated to the officer in a command. I'm reading this in Article 16. It says here that it is subordinated to the commander of the unit in whose strength it is placed. That's what I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Mindua would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I would like to complement the question that was asked by General Tolimir, because Mr. Witness, you often say that you don't know, in answering a question. You say you have no idea about what is asked from you. But here I think that the question should be interesting for you, since I note that in 1995, you were a major in the Zvornik Brigade and that your position was that of assistant to the chief of staff. So in this position, I think that you should have known at least what was the work of the assistant in charge of security. Is that too complicated for you? I really don't know how to ask my question differently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was involved with personnel, and I didn't have to study any documents that referred to the work of other organs in the brigade, and that's why my answers are mostly, I don't know, I didn't study, I didn't read. For me, it is an unknown ground. And despite of the fact that I was involved in the Personnel Affairs, you have to understand that I did not know what other officers did during that period of time, and you also have to bear in mind that before that time and after that time, I never worked in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So if I understand what you just said, as an assistant to the chief of staff within your brigade, you didn't know to whom your other colleagues, the other assistants, were to report. I'm not putting this question based on a theoretical document. I'm asking you based on your experience. Is that too difficult for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can tell you what I know. I did draft reports, as did other organs for their respective levels, operative reports, logistics reports, security reports, personnel reports, a report on morale. I was not in a position to learn how other people wrote their report. I did not have the authority to inspect a report sent by any other organ on any other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right. This is sufficient for me for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question to you, sir. Mr. Tolimir asked you, in his last question: "Could you please tell us who the security organ in your unit was subordinated to? I'm asking you for your answer based on what you know from practice." Are you able to provide us with your knowledge and your recollection about this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security organ was subordinated to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. One moment, please. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in follow-up to Judge Mindua's questions and position, which I share, may I ask you the following question which flows immediately from what you said in lines -- page 6, lines, I think, 24 to 25, through to 7 and 2. You said: "I can tell you what I know. I did draft reports, as did other organs for their respective levels, operative reports, logistical reports, security reports." And the accused is asking you questions regarding management of security organs. What was your practice specifically with regard to the security reports that you drafted, as it's stated here by yourself? There must have been some rules under which you operated or co-operated with the security organs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of security wrote reports on security, and he was the one who sent them to the corps command. As far as I can remember, he also participated in the drafting of operative reports which were daily sent to the corps command by the duty operations officers. That's as much as I can remember at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put another follow-up question to the last one by Judge Nyambe. In your previous answer, you said: "I did draft reports, as did other organs for their respective levels ..." And then you mentioned a list of different reports, operative reports, logistic reports, security reports, personnel reports, report on morale. Can you tell us who drafted these reports to the superior units or persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Duty operations officers drafted those reports. They followed a certain guide-line, and other people wrote reports. The assistant for morale wrote about morale, the assistant for personnel wrote about personnel, the assistant for security wrote about security. Each assistant wrote their part. In other words, we all participated in the drafting of daily operative reports that were sent on a daily basis to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that you drafted, as the assistant for personnel, the reports on personnel matters? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. That was just one segment in the overall report. My contribution consisted of a couple of sentences, and so did the contributions of all the other participants in the drafting of those reports. I was one of the drafters who was in charge of covering the personnel matters. I contributed one to three sentences. If there was something interesting or if I had received an order to cover a certain area, then I would cover that area for the daily reports that were sent to the corps command. My contribution to the operative report were a couple of sentences on the personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To fully understand your answer: All these assistant commanders contributed to a common report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, [as interpreted] all assistants of the chief of staff did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who compiled the final report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The final report was compiled by the duty operations officer in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who signed the final report which was compiled by the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either the brigade commander or the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this final report was sent to which unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sent daily to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 9, line 19, I believe that there should be an "and" following a "Yes." So the sentence should read: "Yes, and all assistants of the chief of staff." So there is an "and" missing from this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This may be your position. I really don't see the difference, but that is perhaps a question of interpretation. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, your question referred to the assistant -- assistants to the commander, and the witness answered "and also the assistants chief of staff," which means that he was referring both to the assistants to the commander as well as to the assistants to the chief of staff. At least that is what I heard in the original Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify the matter with the witness. Sir, once again, my question: "All these assistant commanders contributed to a common report; is that correct?" That was my question. Could you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Assistants to the commander contributed in the writing of that report, and I added to that that the assistants chief of staff also wrote their parts for that common joint report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and I would like to thank the Judges for their questions. I will no longer need the document that is now on the screen, but I would rather call up P1112. This is an instruction on control and command in the security organs. The witness mentioned that document early on yesterday, and he was also asked about that instruction by the investigators. Let's look at the instruction now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, is this the set of instructions that you meant when you said that a set of instructions had arrived at the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I said that some instructions arrived. I didn't see them, and I was not familiar with the contents of those instructions. I only heard that they had arrived, and I believed that it may be this one. I never read it myself. I never learned about its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Prosecutor ever show you these instructions in the proofing sessions?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I don't think that this was ever shown to me. I don't remember, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In that case, I'm going to ask you only this: Can you look at bullet point 2, from which I'm going to quote: "The security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institution of which they form part, but with regard to professional activities, they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command." My question is this: Does this also envisage that security organs in the units are subordinated to the commanders of the units they form a part of and that they are professionally controlled by other organs?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I really don't see how this relates to me. How do these instructions relate to me? I have already told you, and I repeat, I'm not familiar with the contents of these instructions. The only thing I knew at the time is what I already told the investigators, and what I told them was that I had heard on the grape-vine that a set of instructions had arrived at the command. I never saw the text. I never saw how it was worded. I don't know what it regulated. The only thing that was mentioned here and the only thing that I knew was that in addition to the operative reports, the security organs sent either regular or interim reports to the superior command. I don't know whether they did it based on this instruction or some other document, and this is the long and the short of it. This is the only thing that I discussed about this topic with the investigators, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The investigators asked you quite a lot of questions, as did lawyers, about these instructions, and you were asked whether those instructions were a sticking point between the commander and the security organ. If you want me to, I can read you back your answers, if you don't remember. Thank you. However, I just want to ask you, and then you can answer without any further adieu. You don't have to explain at great length. You just tell us how things were, and we will avoid all misunderstandings. Since you said that you don't know, that you didn't read instructions, I quoted from the second bullet point of the set of instructions, where it says that the security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institutions of which they form a part. And my question is this: Did these instructions envisage the same thing as the rules envisaged, and that is that the commander is in charge and responsible for the security organ in his unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the instructions and looking at the rules, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the second part of the sentence, does it say that: "With regard to professional activities, they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command"? Is this centralised control, and does it apply to all security organs in the subordinated lower-ranking units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I don't understand your question. I cannot answer. This is double Dutch to me. I don't know what you're talking about. I'm not familiar with the material. I can't say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you controlled the organs in the lower-ranking units when it came to filling in some forms or delivering data to be filled in two forms, so did you give them instructions as to how they should do this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had people dealing with general affairs in the lower-ranking units who delivered reports to the organ I was a part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And these people, were they subordinated to you or did you ask them to provide only the information you needed in order to report to your superior command? I'm referring to general affairs officers in the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At every point, I was able to ask for any information I needed from these desk officers in charge of general affairs, regardless of what unit was in question. They -- I had direct contact with them. I was able to contact them and ask for the data I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know this. What I'm asking you is whether you commanded these desk officers or whether somebody else commanded them.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period when I was assistant to the chief of staff, I was not in command of any unit or anything. Quite simply, I had no command responsibility, and nor was I able to command anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, yes, I understand you, but for the sake of the transcript: When it comes to these desk officers, were you in command of them or not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When I finish my question, please answer only then so it enters the transcript. When it comes to these desk officers who had to submit data to you, were you commanding these people or not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in command of individual desk officers. They were not subordinate to me, except for the one who worked together with me in the same department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at the last page of this instruction so we can see who signed it and who issued it. You see it was supposed to be signed by the commander, but it was signed on his behalf by General Tolimir. My question is the following: Are you aware whether the word "instruction" - it's a Latin word which we used, unfortunately, instead of using our own word - what does it mean, what does the word "instruction" mean?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, for example, a driving instructor, what does he do?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what "instructions" contain. If you're asking me about driving instructors, they teach people to do certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean, then, something like teaching or training someone, and when it comes to these commands to which this instruction was delivered, is it an instructive document which is supposed to teach people what to do, how to conduct themselves, and to organise relations within the command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I don't recognise your signature, I don't know it, I'm not familiar with it, but you told me now that you signed it. However, when it comes to writing these instructions and -- I don't know anything about it. I find it very difficult to answer your questions. What this word means in Latin, I don't know. I believe that you are familiar with these matters. You were the one who wrote this and signed it, so you are familiar with it. I am not, and so I can't say whether it had an instructive effect on the subordinates or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you say that you are not familiar with any of this, and I quite understand you, do you agree that I should read the last sentence? It says, and I quote: "Forward these instructions and inform of their contents all commanders of units and institutions, down to battalion level." My question is the following: Would all those, down to battalion level, be made aware of the contents of these instructions? Was that the case in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a battalion commander. Whether the battalion commander was made aware of this, I don't know. And as I told you, I was never aware of the contents of these instructions. I don't know whether they were forwarded to all commanders of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you don't know, but I'm asking you whether, in line with this sentence, all commanders, down to battalion level, were supposed to be made aware of these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so, yes, as they were delivered to all units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now again look at document D294, page 13, the fourth paragraph on that page. It's page 17 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar. It's page 16 in English, last passage, and page 13 in Serbian. Thank you, Aleksandar. Well, we can see the fourth paragraph now. It's the second from the bottom. The lawyer is asking: "Did your commander express any concern because he had no control over the military police?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. General, could you please repeat your question? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you were asked whether your commander, because he did not have command over the military police, was he dissatisfied with the situation, did he express any dissatisfaction, and your answer was that, no, you did not observe anything like that. You said, No, I didn't observe that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can repeat that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can you then tell us why the misunderstanding arose that Mr. Manning asked you about? Do you know why there was a misunderstanding between your commander and your security organ, and you asked about this in your testimony and interviews? Just tell us whether you know this or not.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was in the sending of reports. Something is not working properly. Oh, yes. The problem was in the delivery of reports. That's what I understood. And there was some sort of minor misunderstanding, and at one of the meetings, as I told the investigator, it was said that two reports were sent, and then after that there were no problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report to the superior personnel organ in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I received orders from the superior command. It was at monthly intervals, or bimonthly, or every three months, but not every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they oversee your work, or, rather, the superior organs in the superior command of the Drina Corps, did they supervise your work?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have P1108 in e-court. Thank you. This is the second part of your interview with Dean Manning, dated the 27th of June, 2002, and I would now like to see page 53, after we see the first page, in both languages. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see page 53? Thank you. Do you see page 53, the third passage from the bottom and the sixteenth from the top?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We all see pages, but without any page number. Now there's 53. Thank you. I think we need only one. It's exactly the same. We need only one of this page because it's in both languages. The lower part of this page, please. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the third -- sixth passage from the bottom, where it says: "Mihajlo Galic: What do you say to this --" There's something wrong here. It's the first passage on page 53. Thank you. You were asked: "What do you say to the supposition that this operation was planned and carried out exclusively by the Security Service, that is, security officers?" And you say: "I don't know, and I cannot say anything about that, and I cannot assume anything." And then you go on to say in your next reply: "I cannot claim something that I don't know. I cannot confirm something that I'm not aware of." My question is: Did you have the feeling that the investigators and the lawyers wanted you to give opinions, conclusions, and so on about your brigade, and that they were, in fact, trying to put leading questions to you, trying to get you to say things that would be convenient for them?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me -- in the context of all other questions, they asked me this question, and I gave this reply, and I would give the same reply again. If I didn't participate in something or if I wasn't there, I didn't know anything about it, and I would say the same today as I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I know very well what you're saying, but can you say why you were asked this question? Why did they ask you this when they were interviewing you? You can say that you know or that you don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that all that was done because of the proceedings that were conducted before this Tribunal. I suppose that they wanted to obtain information through people who could provide information. I was not one of them; not then, not in the past, not now, not in the future. That's why I provided the type of answers that I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up P1108 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is on the screen. This is the document we have before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I forgot to mention the page number, which is 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at it. I can't read English, but I would like to point your attention to paragraph 3, or perhaps the first paragraph, or perhaps the second paragraph, actually. No, no, no, this document that I have on the screen does not correspond to what I have before me. Page 38, it says you were asked: "Did Drago Nikolic have his own vehicle?" And you say -- we can see it at the bottom, the last paragraph that we can see, or half of it: "Drago Nikolic did have his own vehicle, and that was the security unit vehicle that nobody else used but him. I'm sure that I did not use that vehicle at the time, that's for sure." My question to you is: Did Drago Nikolic, who was the brigade security organ, have a car at his disposal? If he did have a car, was it a car that belonged to the brigade command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ had his own car and used it. There was a vehicle. He had that vehicle. And as I've already said to the investigators, that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us now look at D147, page 16. Thank you. But first let's look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a statement provided by the driver who drove that car. Let's see what he says about all that. D147, this is the statement. Let's look at the third line, where it says "Milorad Bircakovic." Do you know who Milorad Bircakovic is or was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name does ring a bell, but I don't know the man personally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now can we go to page 16 in that same statement, and now on page 16, let us look at the fifth entry from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Milorad Bircakovic says here: "That lasted for two or three months, and then it was decided that the car could not be assigned exclusively to the chief of security ..." After that, "It was used to drive around operatives and those who were in charge of going and checking the battalions ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 17, the second entry from the top of the page. It says here: "You say that the car was assigned for other people to use. Did that include only the military police or was it used by other units as well?" And then Mr. Bircakovic says: "For other units, I believe for the command or for that part of the command."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: This driver from the military police who used to drive that car and who used to drive other commanders from the command, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I don't have any doubts that this man did not drive the security organ vehicle, and I am not questioning the fact that he drove other officers to other units to accomplish certain missions. The vehicles that were normally used by the commander or the chief of staff could be used by other people if there were no other cars available. So it was not a problem for anybody being taken from A to B, but it was a well-known fact which car belongs to the commander, which car belongs to the chief of staff, which belonged to the chief of security. There was also a logistics vehicle. And that's how travel orders were issued. That's as much as I know. Travel papers for the cars were issued in respect of each and every different car in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at what was said on transcript page 9202 on the 9th [as interpreted] of February. Let's see what Mr. Bircakovic stated during his testimony here before the Tribunal. Thank you. That was on the 1st of February, 2011. Thank you. Let's look at line 15. I don't know whether you have that in the Serbian - I don't - where it says, lines 15, 16 and 17, and I quote -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we need a clear record. Are you now quoting from the OTP statement or are you quoting from the transcript of this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm reading from page 9202, lines 14 through 17. This is the transcript from this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is no B/C/S translation because the transcript is only in English, just to clarify. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, that's why I'm going to interpret or translate. I'm going to read line 14: "Later on, there was something that transpired between Drago Nikolic and Pandurevic, who somewhat restricted his right to the vehicle so the vehicle was placed at the disposal of the command. From there on, I drove anybody who needed the vehicle, including Drago Nikolic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was stated by the driver who used to drive that vehicle for which you say that it belonged to Drago Nikolic. He testified here. He said he was a member of the police and that he drove everybody in the command. My question is this: Did the driver ever drive you? Do you know if he ever drove any of the other officers in the command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of my previous answers, I said that any vehicle [as interpreted] could drive any of the officers. Whether he drove me or not, I suppose he did, but I don't remember. It was such a long time ago, I really can't remember any of the days, dates, or routes that I was driven on. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't remember, I will not insist. You heard what the person said whose job that was. I would kindly ask the e-court to display P1112. Thank you. Thank you. I apologise, I misspoke. I need D41. Thank you. I apologise to the e-court. D41. Thank you. Now we have the document in front of us. It was issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 9th of July, 1995. It was signed by Assistant Commander Major General Zdravko Tolimir. In the first part of the document, it says that: "The president of Republika Srpska has been informed of successful combat operations around Srebrenica ..." It says in the second paragraph that he is satisfied, and in the third it says that he ordered that in the follow-up combat operations, and so on and so forth. In the fourth paragraph, we see an instruction, as it were, and it reads: "In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, you must issue an order to all combat units participating in combat operations around Srebrenica to offer maximum protection and safety to all UNPROFOR members and the civilian Muslim population. You must order subordinate units to refrain from destroying civilian targets unless forced to do so because of strong enemy resistance. Ban the torching of residential buildings, and treat the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949." And then you can see the signature of Major General Zdravko Tolimir. My question to you is this: Since it says here that an order should be issued to all subordinated units to behave according to this instruction, do you know whether an order was, indeed, issued to subordinated units to act in accordance with the Geneva Conventions? I'm talking about those units that participated in combat around Srebrenica together with your unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, how am I supposed to know whether that order was issued to the units participating in combat around Srebrenica, the order based on this document? I don't know. I was not there. I don't know. I see what you see. There is a document sent to somebody, and that person was supposed to do something. Whether they did that or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask you whether you knew. I asked you whether you are familiar with this, and you answered the way you did. This was sent to the forward command post of the Drina Corps, to Gvero and Krstic, as you can see. And in the second line of the last paragraph, it says: "You must issue an order to all combat units participating in combat operations." And based on this, my question is as follows: Did all commanders who participated in combat around Srebrenica receive an order or, rather, an invitation to act in accordance with Geneva Conventions? What I'm asking you is: Does this document mean this? I'm not asking you whether you received -- they received it or not.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see and read this document, I would say, yes, that was what was asked of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this contrary to what they asked you before, and that is whether security organs organised or that -- could they have organised all that in view of the fact that they had issued a document to the effect that all combat units around Srebrenica should be made familiar with this order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about the mindset of the people who were involved in this process. Something is contrary to something else, but I cannot be the judge of that. I can't tell you what's contrary to what. This is very -- a very complex issue for me. I can't tell you whether this was conveyed or not, and so on and so forth. The investigators must have had a concept that they followed, I'm sure. And here we have a document ordering units to do this or that. What is the true [as interpreted] in that, I really don't know. This is really a tall order for me. I really can't tell how people behaved and based on what they based their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you talked about contradictions, for the record, could you tell us whether this document was authentic, whether it was certified by the encoder who sent it from the Main Staff or the person who received it at the other end? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can see a stamp, which means that the encryptors sent it, but we can't see whether it arrived at the address of the addressee. I suppose it did. This is a photocopy. I really don't know how this was sent. But I can see a stamp in the right-hand-side corner, so this is a stamp indicating that encryptors received the document and dispatched it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking you whether you knew this from your experience, as you received telegrams, whether this one was an authentic telegram. Thank you. Your Honours, I have no questions for this witness -- no further questions. Witness, thank you for coming to testify here. I apologise for putting the questions I had to put for the requirements of these proceedings. Thank you. God bless you. I wish you a speedy recovery and a safe journey home. I thank you, and I wish to thank everyone who assisted us in the course of this testimony. Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Hasan, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I don't have any questions for re-examination, just a couple of housekeeping matters that we can do either once the witness is dismissed or at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination and your testimony here in this courtroom in this trial. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague again and to testify and to help us to establish the facts. Now you are free to return to your normal activities and your normal life. I see you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to have a stain left. When this institution contacted me, I spoke to people, and never at any point did I intend to say I didn't want to come here. The problem was my health. In view of certain things I had to do with a doctor, and certain medical examinations I had to undergo outside my place of residence, I wanted to delay my arrival. This was done, and I am grateful. It was -- I received a promise that I would be able to go home on Wednesday so that I will be able to go for further medical examinations, but -- I don't know what the name of the letter is that I received, but I did not think I would receive such a letter based on my contacts with the Tribunal, and this worries me. It was something I did not expect to receive, because I never said that I would not respond or come to the Tribunal. It was only because of my health that there were those delays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. I think the matter is resolved completely. There's no problem for you at all. You are now free to return to your home. Thank you very much, again, including this explanation. You are now released from the courtroom. Thank you very much, again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to P1115, an e-mail was sent out regarding a revised translation that has come in, and we'd like to have that -- permission to replace the revised translation with the one that was on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this has to be granted. We are grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, second, a similar -- a similar request, and that's in relation to P1124, which is the IKM log-book. That was admitted through PW-057, and at the time there was an error noticed in the translation, which has now been corrected, and so there is a revised translation that we would also like to up-load and replace the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that will be appreciated by the Defence as well. It should be done as proposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps it's a good time to take the next break so that my colleague can come in preparation for the next witness, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Indeed, we should have our first break now. We will resume 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, especially to you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Welcome to the courtroom again. Is the Prosecution in the position to give us some more information about future witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first witness, Mr. Hedley, 198, he is what they call a scenes-of-crime investigator who was taking part in the exhumations and the review of materials from the Kravica warehouse, and he was a -- we offered his report in through 94 bis, which was not accepted by the Court. So if I can have some time to speak with Mr. Gajic to see if the material in there is contested - I'm not really sure it is - so that we can make a further decision on whether we need to call him or not, but that we will be able to make that decision this week. Then the other person, Mr. de Koeijer, it -- is a Dutch forensic person that works in the Dutch lab here, that examined a document that you have seen in court. It's the military police log of the Zvornik Brigade Military Police Company, and his report examines that log and identifies eraser marks at key places, and he concludes that certain places were erased and identifies that other letters were written over the erasure marks. I can't recall if you've actually seen that document or not, and -- excuse me, Judge Nyambe, let me get in there too. Though that document, you can actually see the erasure marks and you can see the marks that were written in them, so I will get that original and show that to Mr. Gajic and to you and perhaps that will resolve that issue, because my recollection is he just basically has a report that tells you what you can see. It's important because it has to do with military police, and prisoners at Orahovac, and -- you know, which is, of course, an issue, that are overseen by security. You're hearing a lot about these issues. So -- and that's 65 ter number 642, that -- that particular -- is that -- the report. Yeah, I'm sure the log is actually in evidence. Mr. Gajic would like to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask Mr. McCloskey to slow down because the interpreters are having difficulty keeping up with him, and that's why I'm on my feet. I can read what Mr. McCloskey is saying on the transcript in English, but the general is not receiving the entire message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful, and I only regret that you're not on your hands. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And the roster I speak of that was the subject of the report is P1754, so we'll bring that in and let everybody take another look at it, and perhaps we can resolve it. It's an important document, but a relatively simple issue. That may resolve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, these two witnesses, you will be in a position to clarify the position with the Defence by the end of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In discussions with them and perhaps if I have some time to bring that document in to see -- to get your viewpoint on it, then we may -- we may render that issue moot because, as I recall, you can actually see the subject of his report. And if you can see that, then it's not really an issue. But if it isn't, then we'll have to call him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- or request that he be called. Then the other four witnesses that were the subject of the footnote, these are women from Srebrenica who we've taken 92 bis statements as part of a larger group of women from Srebrenica. And the Trial Chamber has, some time back, identified some glitches or inconsistencies in those statements, and we have -- we need to just buckle down and study those inconsistencies and see if we can resolve them without too much resources. And if we can, we'll fix them and get them in front of you. If we can't, we may have to withdraw them. But I -- again, this week is something we will get this done by. It's just a matter of buckling down and getting that done. So this week, we will resolve all of these for you, and I'm glad we're able -- I'm helpful [sic] that you've helped remind us of these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This will then be the basis of our planning for the remainder of the Prosecution case and for possible 98 bis proceedings. We will come back to that. Thank you very much. Is the next witness ready, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. He is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Janc. Please sit down. I don't think there is any need to have a further oath to be taken from you. We have seen you several times here in the courtroom. But I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of the first day of your testimony still applies for this part of your examination as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have the floor for your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good afternoon everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Janc, and welcome back yet again.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wanted to have you - and you know this - to testify concerning certain intercepts that were obtained by Croatian authorities. Let me begin by asking you whether you've had an opportunity to review a number of these intercepts with a view towards establishing whether or not they are reliable, in fact.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about when you became involved in reviewing this material for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I started with a detailed review of these intercepts and related material sometimes at the beginning of February this year, but also before I already came across most of these intercepts and material, which I re-reviewed again in relation to my testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of assessing the reliability of this material, did you -- can you just tell us, briefly, what sorts of things you did, in terms of looking at the intercepts, either the content of the intercepts, the dates, the circumstances that they speak about, those kinds of things? Could you tell us, briefly, what kinds of material you looked at in order to evaluate their reliability?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, the intercept, itself, was important, and everything what was on the -- what was written on that intercept, beginning from the date and time when it was recorded. And the most important part was, of course, the content of the intercept, itself, because from the content, you could get an idea of what -- what perhaps happened at a particular time and place, who was involved in it, what kind of incident took place, and this kind of information you can get from the content of the intercept, itself. Based on this information, we can then compare or find supporting documents; for example, certain reports from a particular date which would, for example -- describing a certain event from the intercept, itself, and this would corroborate, then, the intercept. In this way, we can then say that certain intercepts are reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to find corroborating material or review corroborating material with respect to these particular intercepts? And when I say "these particular," I'm distinguishing them from intercepts that originated with the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or intercepts that originated with the MUP, or other agencies that engaged in that conduct. So in terms of this material, were you able to find corroborating -- corroboration?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. And today we are talking about the intercepts which were intercepted by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, and I could find and review the corroborative material in relation to these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And before we go into that, let me just ask you: In terms of the material that you compared these intercepts against, did you consider material that was independent of those intercepts or related to those intercepts, as it were? If you could just briefly describe the relationship of the material that you used to corroborate the intercepts with the intercepts themselves, so the Trial Chamber has an idea of what kind of project you undertook.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. I reviewed the material which is independent of these intercepts, and such documents would be, for example, documents drafted by different international organisations at the time; for example, UNPROFOR reports or daily sitreps. Then there would be different reports or documents from the VRS, itself. Then also diaries of individuals involved in these meetings or incidents were important. Then, for example, there were also intercepts from the BiH Army, who intercepted, for example, the same conversation as the Croatian authorities did, and these were, basically, the documents which I reviewed and considered for my testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I would like to show you a selection of these intercepts. Mr. President, I have a packet that I would like to share with the Trial Chamber, which I think would make it easier to follow the testimony of Mr. Janc. We also have e-court, but I think it's also helpful to have these packets which I'd like to pass up to the Court. They do contain, and I should raise this, they do contain some material that has not yet been added to the Prosecution's 65 ter list. So it's the material with the 65 ter number with the star next to it to indicate that the Trial Chamber -- and I've, of course, provided Mr. Gajic with a copy of the same packet. I don't know whether or not Mr. Gajic has an objection to the Trial Chamber receiving the packet, itself, which is, I think, a separate issue than whether or not it is used with the witness. But I assume that if he has any objection when it's used with the witness, he can raise that. With that proviso, I would like to hand it up to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position on that? May that be used during the testimony of Mr. Janc? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as regards the first issue raised by the Prosecutor, of course, we do not object that the package we received also be delivered to the Chamber and the witness, if necessary. As for the documents to be added to the 65 ter list, I think there are just a few of these documents. I had a chance of looking at them. Unfortunately, they have not all been translated into Serbian. We do not, at this point, object to their being included on the 65 ter list. All we ask is that the OTP, when showing these documents in the courtroom, bear in mind that there are no translations of these documents, and, of course, that a translation be made as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This will be the usual procedure, of course. And if some documents are not yet on the 65 ter exhibit list, then you will have the opportunity to object or to comment on the motion of the Prosecution to add it. The binders you have prepared should be delivered to the Chamber, with the assistance of the Court Usher, to the Defence and to the witness. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a brief question, first of all, for the OTP. I think it's in the interests of all concerned to hear the official reply. When Witness PW-070 testified, we received a bundle of documents in a binder. All these documents have their 65 ter number, but now on this Prosecution list, I can see that only a few of the documents from this bundle, about one-seventh, are on that list. So what I would like to know is whether the OTP intends to ask that these documents be admitted at some later stage of the proceedings or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's a fair question. As I mentioned, the object of the testimony was to establish the reliability of these intercepts. The intercepts that are on the exhibit list are all intercepts that are derived from the list that Mr. Gajic refers to, so they all have 65 ter numbers. The documents that don't have 65 ter numbers, many of them are documents that simply relate to matters that are discussed in the intercept or otherwise go to the reliability of the intercept, and that's why you can see some documents don't have 65 ter numbers, and that's what I intended to use with the witness to establish reliability. In terms of their admissibility, ultimately, I think it would be helpful, certainly, for the Trial Chamber to have that so the Trial Chamber can see for itself whether or not the information contained in the intercept is corroborated to the extent that Mr. Janc testifies. But at the same time, I think merely the explanation that's given as to the reliability should be sufficient -- a sufficient-enough basis to establish it, so we can resolve the question of admissibility at a later point. But I think at this point, since the Defence doesn't have an objection to the use of the documents, we can probably just proceed and then resolve the admissibility issues later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, would you agree to this proposal to decide on a case-by-case basis when it comes to the use of certain documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President. That would be the usual procedure. However, I am afraid that Mr. Vanderpuye didn't really understand my question. I think that it was Mr. Vanderpuye. I don't know who, exactly, examined Witness PW-070. We received 74 documents in a binder, and my question referred to these documents only, not the documents in the binder we received today. This is very important because the Defence needs to prepare, and we would simply like to hear from the Prosecutor what they intend to do with the rest of these documents; nothing else, well, to show you -- to illustrate what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I appreciate the illustration. I think I now understand the issue more clearly. With respect to the admissibility of this group of intercepts, that is, the one that was referred to in other testimony, that collection, we're seeking at this point to admit the intercepts that are on my exhibit list. With respect to the remainder of those intercepts, we're not tendering them at this point. They may become relevant at a later point in the case, depending on whether or not there's a Defence case, depending on what comes up in cross-examination, but for these purposes today, and probably into tomorrow a little bit, all we're seeking to admit pursuant to the testimony of Mr. Janc are the intercepts that are on my exhibit list. I think there are probably 18 or 19 of them. And that's it for now, and that's it pursuant to Mr. Janc's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We fully understand you. When you refer to your exhibit list, you are referring to the Prosecution's exhibit list for the current witness, Mr. Janc, to use with him in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we now understand the procedure you want to follow. You have the floor. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I'd just like to start with 65 ter 5536, if we could have that one on the screen. Your Honours, you should find this one, with any luck, right under tab 1 of your binders, and you'll see the English, which should be followed by a B/C/S translation, and then it would be followed by some other corroborating material which you can see referred to in the index of the packet. Mr. Janc, I take it you've had an opportunity to review this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we'll note that this one is dated 18 June 1994. It's at 2200 hours, and it records here that: "On more than one occasion, General Kelecevic intervened with Colonel Zdravko Tolimir (chief of security in the Main Staff of the VRS), to intervene with President Karadzic and Stanisic, to place under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps a special forces unit of the MUP ..." Now, with respect to this particular intercept, you notice here that the designation is "Colonel Zdravko Tolimir" as the chief of security. Were you able to find any documents relating to Mr. Tolimir's rank status in around this period of time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, Mr. Zdravko Tolimir was still a colonel, and the significance of this intercept is related to the one which will be -- the one after this one, which is a few days after 18 of June, when General Tolimir, actually at that time colonel, became a Major General Tolimir. So that's the significance, so -- but for this particular intercept, we don't have any corroborative document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 5537, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this intercept we can see again it's dated 29 June 1994. If we look to the second paragraph of this intercept, we can see that there's a reference to a decree of President Karadzic with respect to the promotion of certain military officers. And, in particular, we can see, in the fourth line down in the English, and it should be about the fourth line or so -- fifth line from the bottom in the B/C/S, we can see a reference to Zdravko Tolimir, and, in particular, it says that: "Pursuant to a decree of President Karadzic, the following people were promoted:" And it says. "... to the general major rank, Colonels Mico Grubor, Zdravko Tolimir, and Jovan Maric, Stavan Tomic ..." And so on and so forth. Was this the document that you were referring to concerning the promotion of Zdravko Tolimir from colonel to major general or general major?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this was the intercept I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to find any corroboration with respect to this intercept as concerns the promotion of Zdravko Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There is a decree of the President Karadzic from 20 -- dated 28th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is to show you this document and see if it's the one you're referring to, and it is 65 ter 5525.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, I take it that these documents now mentioned are under tab 1 in the binder we have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, they're all under tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here, we have a Decree Number 01-1275/94, dated 28 June 1994, and it refers to a number of officers that are exceptionally promoted. It says: "To the rank of Lieutenant General:" And it names Major Generals Milovanovic, Manojlo; Gvero, Milan; Djukic, Djordje. And then it names on the second page, and in the B/C/S it's just -- it would just be -- just around the photocopy line near the bottom of the page, we can see here a reference to the following colonels being promoted to the rank of major. And you can see here the second person listed here is "Zdravko Tolimir, son of Stanko, assistant commander for security and intelligence of the VRS." It says "General Staff." It should be, probably, "Main Staff." But is this the document you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One -- I think one correction is needed. You misspoke. Line 5 of page 43, "promoted to the rank of major." I think you wanted to say "to the rank of major general."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, major general or general major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said "Major" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and it is recorded in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this the document that you were referring to, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the -- if we go to the next page, we can see here that it is from the president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic; yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, I would like to tender all of these documents under tab 1, beginning with: 65 ter 5525, this the intercept from the 28th of June, 1994, referring to the promotion of General Tolimir; the document which is 5536, that's the intercept from 18 June, which indicates that General Tolimir at that time was a colonel; 65 ter 5537, which indicates -- which refers to, rather, the -- a decree of the president; and there is one other document I'd like to show Mr. Janc. The last of these documents is 3928, but I'll put that up on the screen and show it to him first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We want to see 65 ter 3928.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, have you had an opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see here that this one is dated from the -- dated, rather, 28th June 1994, which is the same day as the document we've just seen. The intercept, rather.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's also the same date as the decree that we've seen, issued by President Karadzic, promoting then Colonel Tolimir to the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It's just a small correction, actually. This intelligence report is dated on the day when the decree of the President Karadzic was issued, but the intercept is the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right. So it's -- this the same day as the decree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And on that day, if we look at the bottom of this document, we can see how it is signed. I'm sorry, we'll have to go to the second page in both.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, we have a typed signature of General Major Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does this corroborate the information that you reviewed in relation to the intercept, in terms of Mr. Tolimir's rank prior to the 28th of June, 1994, and following June 28th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, since this is a quite complicated procedure, I would like to ask you if you have any objections to tendering these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any objections to admitting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These four documents, 65 ter 5525, 5536, 5537 and 3928, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 5525 shall be assigned Exhibit P2437. 65 ter number 5536 shall be assigned Exhibit P2438. 65 ter number 5537 shall be assigned Exhibit P2439. And 65 ter 03928 shall be assigned Exhibit P2440. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I'd like to show you some of the documents I have here under tab 2, and we'll start with 65 ter 5538, which is an intercept from 13 July 1994, at 22 hundred 18 minutes of that day. Have you had a chance to look at this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see here that the intercept talks about a meeting that was supposed to occur between General Tolimir and General Van Baal on the 12th of July in Gorazde; yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to find any information concerning the content of this intercept that corroborates it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There is several documents and a portion of a diary of General Ratko Mladic where we can find corroborative information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the diary of General Mladic, what, specifically, were you able to identify that corroborates what we see in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Actually, there was a meeting on 11th of July, 1994, with General Mladic and members of the UNPROFOR present, and part of the diary from that date shows that it was mentioned or discussed that General Van Baal will be going to Gorazde with General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could take a look, please, at P1424. I think we'll have to go to page 206 in the B/C/S, and hopefully it will be 196 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what we have on the screen now, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a diary of General Ratko Mladic and the note -- notes which start on 11th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can continue up to the next page, we can see here there's some note concerning freedom of movement of UNPROFOR. Did you have an opportunity to review that, in light of the content of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having reviewed it, does it support what is written in the intercept as concerns a proposed topic of a meeting between General Van Baal and officers of the VRS regarding the freedom of movement for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page. I'm sorry, we need to go to 209. It would be 199 in the English. 209 in the B/C/S and 199 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we can see at the top of the page item number 4, which is a note written by General Mladic, and did you have an opportunity to review this particular entry in relation to the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how did you -- how do you view this particular entry, in terms of the reliability of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is a part what I was referring before, where it says that General Van Baal and General Tolimir will be going to Gorazde. It doesn't say when, exactly, but we can see from the intercept that General Van Baal tried to go to Gorazde on 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell from the entry in the note-book -- or diary, I'm sorry, when this was made, this particular entry that we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: If we followed the diary, itself, and we have been going page by page now, we could see where we started, that it is a meeting from 11th of July, 1994, and this meeting goes for a while. And the diary doesn't shows any change in date up until this page, so it must have been still on 11 of July, 1995 -- 1994, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know if this diary reflects a date between the 11th -- I should say following the 11th of July, 1994?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a change in date a few pages after this one, and the next date is then 13 of July. So we have no entries or nothing was written on 12th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So if we go over to page 204 in the English, and I think it will be 214 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need 204 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, is this the entry that you're referring to that we see here at the top of the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this is the page where the date changed to 13 of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your conclusion is, then, what with respect to the entry concerning the meeting or the future meeting between Van Baal and Tolimir that we saw at page 199 in the English and 209, I believe, in the B/C/S just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: My conclusion is that that meeting supposed to take place on 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could take a look now at 65 ter -- well, actually, this is a document that was not on the Prosecution's original 65 ter list, Mr. President. As you can see, I've identified that in the packet before the Trial Chamber. It is a document that is from UNPROFOR. In particular, it's from General Van Baal, and I believe that it relates directly to the content of the intercept at issue. I don't know whether or not General Tolimir has an objection to this particular document, and I don't believe we have a translation of it. However, I can -- if it's required, I can certainly articulate the reason why I'd like to use it, or, rather, its relevance to the intercept in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have any concern to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list, even without a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I have no translation, could Mr. Vanderpuye establish with this witness whether General Mladic entered in his diary observations he heard from others, those he spoke with, or whether he noted down actual events that occurred on a certain day in his -- where he was present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would propose that you, Mr. Vanderpuye - and I take the word of Mr. Tolimir into account - use this document, and later we decide about adding this document to the 65 ter list and a possible admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
