utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I think once you see it, that will resolve a lot of issues. It's 65 ter 744. And as -- yes, we don't have a translation, so let me just read a little bit into the record so that General Tolimir can familiarise himself, to some extent, with its content. It is a letter that is addressed to Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic, chief of staff, and it says: "Headquarters of the SR Army, Pale." And it's dated 12 July 1994. If we go to the second page of the document, we will see that it is signed by Brigadier General Van Baal. What I'd like to focus on, in particular, is the previous page for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I would like to ask Mr. Janc first: Do you recognise the document, and have you had a chance to review it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, for both.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, in summary, what this document -- or how this document, rather, relates to the intercept that we've just seen? The intercept was 65 ter 5538.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the actual complaint from General Van Baal to the VRS, General Manojlo Milovanovic, about the incident that happened in Rogatica when he was stopped at check-point by the VRS and he couldn't proceed his trip towards Gorazde because his personal belongings were supposed to be checked by the VRS. And in the intercept, itself, we can see that this is part of the content of the intercept, where it says that General Van Baal returned back to Sarajevo after refusing to have his personal belongings searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the third paragraph of this document, and here we have, in the middle of the paragraph, it says, for General Tolimir's benefit: "The commander, Captain Zoran, appeared there after five minutes with the necessary information." And he says: "I personally spoke with him. He also insisted on the searching. He excluded my personal belongings from the search. Once more, I told him that I had been personally involved in all negotiations with the BSA HQ on the matter of freedom of movement. Captain Zoran once more stated that he had firm orders to search personal belongings. These were direct orders from General Mladic, he said." In the last paragraph -- well, I'm sorry, the second-to-last paragraph on the page, he then says: "I concluded that we had a different opinion on this point and that I would complain about this humiliating procedure, unacceptable to UNPROFOR, and that I had to turn back to Sarajevo." In particular, what he's written here, how does that relate to the substance of the intercept, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This, as I just explained, confirms the fact that he was, indeed, stopped at Rogatica check-point, and he returned back to Sarajevo after refusing to -- his personal belongings to be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you one other document. That's 65 ter 7445. Mr. President, this is another document that was not on the Prosecution's original 65 ter list, but for the same reasons, I would like to use it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should proceed in the same way as with the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't believe we have a translation of this one either, so I'll read a little bit of it into the record to familiarise General Tolimir with its contents. This is a document which says "From," at the very top, "UNMO LO Team Pale to UNPROFOR HQ Zagreb," and then it says -- it gives the date, "18 July," I believe, "2030 hours," "182030B July 94." The date on the document, itself, says "July 18, 1994," and it says "Headquarters of the RS Army." "To: UNPROFOR Command, Zagreb, Lieutenant General De Lapresle." And it says "To: UNPROFOR Command, Sarajevo." "Attention: Brigadier General Van Baal." If we go to the second-to-last paragraph of this document, or at least down the page, we can see that this document came from the Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic, to whom the complaint was previously addressed, and he says in that second-to-last paragraph: "I want to express my regret to General Van Baal and to apologise for the inconvenience he had undergone."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review this document as well, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you find that it supported or not the intercept in question?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, it supported the intercept in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you another document. It's 65 ter 7446. Mr. President, it's subject to the same circumstances as the others, as you can see indicated in the packet. This one's in French, and it has a B/C/S translation, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review this document, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in reviewing this document, were you able to find if it corroborated or supported the intercept that we're dealing with now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: We'll see that the meeting which is supposed to take place in Gorazde with General -- between General Van Baal and General Tolimir will be discussed in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see on this document that it is dated 11 July 1994?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And is that consistent with the information in the intercept thus far, up until this point?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Up until this point, I don't think so, but later on we'll see that there is written the date of 12th of July, when this meeting will take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go over to item number big 3 -- Roman numeral III(A). That will be on page 2 in the English, and it should be on page 2 in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that there is no English, but the French --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to review this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the reference you made concerning the date -- or the reference that you found concerning the date of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, in paragraph A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And how does this relate to the intercept in question?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It says here that a meeting will take place between General Van Baal and General Tolimir on 12th of July in Gorazde in relation to the death of the British soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that consistent with what's recorded in the intercept as concerns the meeting that was to transpire between General Tolimir and General Van Baal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: On 12 of July, General Van Baal was on his way down to Gorazde, and he returned back to Sarajevo because he refused to be -- to be checked at check-point. And the intercept, itself, reflects this information, that he was supposed to meet General Tolimir in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you seen any other references to the circumstances of the death of a British soldier, as is indicated here, that was to be discussed on or about 12 July in Gorazde pursuant to this planned meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a reference to this same issue in Mladic's diary which we have just seen before, so the same information is in his diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you consider this together with the diary and the other documents, in terms of the reliability of the intercept that we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And if you put all of them together, we are getting more and more information about certain events. And in this case, we can see that the intercept, itself, is just talking that he was -- I mean, General Van Baal was on the way down to Gorazde. We don't see for what reason. But from other corresponding documents, we can get more information about what this meeting was about, and this is how you put several different documents together and you get more and more information. And also this is the way how to corroborate and -- corroborate the intercepts, itself, and to put them -- reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you one other document, and this is 65 ter 7447. And -- okay, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And we can see here that this is an intercepted conversation taken by the Sarajevo SDB Sector of the MUP of the BiH, and it's dated 13 July 1994, and it's timed at 2215 hours, and it's between General Van Baal and General Mladic. And here we see -- have you had an opportunity to review this particular intercept, first?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you just tell us, just in general terms, what it's about and what it concerns?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is an intercepted conversation by the MUP Sarajevo on the same date and, according to information on this intercept, at about the same hour than the conversation from the Croatian intercept. And I reviewed this document, and I can conclude that this is the same conversation as it is -- as it was recorded by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, because I'm sure everyone will be wondering: Here we see a reference to the time of 1400 hours: "Tomorrow afternoon at Pale, 1400 hours." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the other intercept, 5538, we see here: "14 July at 1600 hours in Pale"; that is, to meet with General Tolimir or General Gvero. And then on the intercept we have on the screen in front of us, we see General Mladic say: "I think it would be better if it took place at 1500 hours." So we have, between the two intercepts, three basically different times, one proposed at 1400, one at 1500, and then in the Croatian intercept, at 1600. Can you tell us how you took that -- if you took that into account at all, in terms of assessing the reliability of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I spotted this discrepancy, and I can say that discrepancies are quite common when you are reviewing the intercepts which were intercepted by two different sources. For example, in this case, one intercept was intercepted by the Government of the Republic of Croatia, and the other one by the BiH side. Why this difference is there in this time, I would say several reasons it might be for that, because, first of all, the intercept which we have on the screen, the BiH intercept, is the actual transcript of the whole conversation, whereas on the other side we have just the summary of the Croatian intercept. So this might be one reason why someone was not that precise when putting summary together. So also some other reasons might be behind. And in this case, I would say the most common problem would be that Croatians were so far away that they couldn't hear, perhaps, the conversation clear enough to establish what they are talking, and that's also, perhaps, the reason why, on the other hand, the BiH side could hear this conversation better and they could put this information into this intercept differently. So -- but the gist of the conversation, itself, is the same, so we can say that there is much more discrepancies in these two intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you consider the discrepancies significant, in terms of evaluating the reliability of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: No, not in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender these documents just as a matter of record. I don't know whether or not the Defence objects to it. If they don't, then I would submit -- I would ask for them to be admitted now. But if they do, then we can discuss it. They were 65 ter 70 -- 7444 through 7447, and the intercept, itself, which was 65 ter 5538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are there any objections to add these documents, the four mentioned documents, to the 65 ter exhibit list and to admit them into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I do have an objection. The Prosecutor is speaking of intercepts, whereas we can see in the intercepts that these are translations from English. So let him tell us whether it was the English who intercepted these conversation or whether it was Bosniaks, Croats. There are many differences among them, and some have been translated, some not. I cannot come to any conclusion just by looking at them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I understood that the intercept is that one of the 13th of July, 1994. The original is obviously Croatian, because the English text has, in the heading, the remark "Translation." This is what I take from this document, which should be 65 ter 5538. This is the only intercept Mr. Vanderpuye just dealt with during this part of the examination of Mr. Janc. The others were other documents. Two of them don't have a translation yet. And, therefore, those documents without a translation, of course, can only be marked for identification, pending translation. That is clear. But in relation to adding them to the 65 ter exhibit list and admission -- admissibility, in principle, I would like to know the position of the Defence. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that what Mr. Tolimir is referring to is the document we see on the screen, 65 ter 7447. We will see, in the heading on the right-hand side, it says: "Translation from English." I think that this is the element General Tolimir was referring to. This has not been clarified in the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it be scrolled down, the English text, please. We want to see -- no, up, up. We want to see the heading. I see the English translation and not translation -- oh, yes: "Translation from English." Mr. Vanderpuye, could you please clarify that with the witness? In the heading I see: "English translation" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and further down on the right side: "Translation from English."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The explanation, I think, can be found in the fact that if you look immediately beneath where it says "Van Baal" and "Mladic," you will see a reference to the conversation occurring with the assistance of a translator. So the conversation between Van Baal and Mladic is mediated by a translator, because Van Baal, presumably, doesn't speak B/C/S and spoke English, and that's what gets translated in the MUP intercept so that it could be understood by the relevant authorities to which this document would normally go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, would that be your understanding of this entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct, this is also my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If something is translated, should it say in the document that it is a translation from English? This is a transcript. There's something wrong here. Why does it say: "Translation from English"? Did they get documents from someone else and translate them or did they actually make the tapes, the audio recordings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. To be honest, I don't think -- I think we just have a disagreement with respect to the meaning of the term, as is indicated in this document: "Translation from English." I don't know that -- I don't know that there's any answer that can be given to General Tolimir, because that question would apply regardless of whether or not this intercept reflected translation from English or not. It could apply in any circumstance with respect to any intercept which could be translated from any language at any time. So I don't think there's any answer that can be given to General Tolimir with respect to that question. However, I think Mr. Janc has identified -- or I should say confirmed at least a reasonable understanding of what the term has indicated, just based on the face of the document, itself, and I think that's a sufficient-enough basis to be able to use it with him, in terms of, in particular, its relationship to the intercept which is recorded by Croatian authorities, really, within minutes of this one, a completely separate authority. So -- but to that extent, I think it satisfies, I would submit, the burden of admissibility at this point. If General Tolimir has questions as to how it could have been recorded or whether it could have been obtained from other sources, I think those are appropriate questions to put during the course of cross-examination or, perhaps, are issues that can be raised in a submission with respect to the weight to be attributed to the document, but I don't think it's an admissibility question at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you get the floor, but I would like to draw your attention to this sentence in brackets beneath the words "Van Baal" and "Mladic," the two names. In the English translation, it's written: "(Conversation conducted with the help of an interpreter of General Van Baal)." That could be an explanation as just -- Mr. Vanderpuye did it. You have the floor, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. All conversations conducted by UN officers were interpreted. This is the first time that it says on the transcript: "Interpretation from English." I don't know how the document was drafted. You should ask the one who processed other documents. Could, perhaps, Mr. Vanderpuye tell us whether the entire document is a translation from English or are just Mr. Van Baal's words interpreted, because all officers who were in Bosnia spoke a foreign language and all of their conversation and words had to be translated or interpreted. But this is the first time ever in any of the document that it is specified that the words are an interpretation or a translation from English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't dispute General Tolimir's observation that we have here a specific -- or an explicit, rather, reference in the document to the fact that it's translated from English. There's -- like I said, there's no answer to how much of it is translated, whether it was just Van Baal, whether General Mladic spoke English, whether or not it was captured by some third party in English, or translated into English and then fed to the MUP. There's simply no way to answer that question, but I think, as I mentioned, that the explanation that Mr. Janc has indicated is one that, on its face, is a reasonable explanation. And what we're talking about here, in terms of the admissibility of the document, is, really, what's on its face, prima facie, not relevance and reliability and probative value, which I think is clear. It's clearly probative with respect to the intercept that is not disputed, in terms of its authenticity, given the prior testimony in this case, and it directly speaks to the issues in that intercept and directly relates to the reliability of that intercept. So it's relevant, it's probative, and, on its face, is reliable enough to be admitted. So that's my argument at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this document, 65 ter 5538, is already on the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Like the Prosecution, the Chamber can't find an explanation why there is this entry: "Translation from English." There may be many explanations, but at the moment we are only dealing with admissibility, which has a quite low threshold. If we look at this document together with the other documents shown to the witness, we will receive this document into evidence without giving weight to that at the moment. That will be done by the Chamber at a later stage, if we really can rely on this document. But it will be part of the whole package of documents in evidence, to give weight to that at a later stage. It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. We need the document number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 5538 shall be assigned Exhibit P2441. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we have to deal with the four documents which are not yet in the 65 ter exhibit list used with this witness. Are there any concerns to add them to the 65 ter exhibit list, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence does not have any objections to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Leave is granted to add these four documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. And I take it that you are tendering these four documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President. It occurs to me, though, that there might be some confusion in the record, and that is that the document that you have in e-court now is 65 ter 7447. It is not 5538. I just wasn't sure if maybe there was some confusion about that. 5538 is the Croatian intercept, but that's not this document. It's another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Mr. Vanderpuye. We mixed up the two numbers. We didn't discuss the intercept, which is 65 ter 5538, and this is now in evidence. We discussed -- and the concern of Mr. Tolimir was in relation to the other intercept, which is - one moment -- please help me. Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: His concern was in relation to this particular intercept, which is 7447, which is a corroborating document to 65 ter 5538. So the principal intercept is 5538. This is the Croatian intercept. A document that's used to corroborate the reliability or demonstrate the reliability of that intercept is this intercept, which is in a BiH MUP intercept, which was recorded very close in time to the Croatian one, but it is not -- it is a separate agency, it's a separate thing altogether. And it's being offered as corroboration for the Croatian intercept. The one that -- so the Croatian intercept has no indication that it's translated from English; none. It's only this corroborating document that does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we can resolve this problem very easily if I ask Mr. Tolimir if there are any objections to the admission of the other documents used with the witness, all those under tab 2 of the binder. Are there any other objections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have already said that the Defence does not have any objections, save for the document 65 ter 07447 [as interpreted], which, in our view, is not an intercept, but a translated conversation. That is our opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that case, we will receive into evidence the document 65 ter 7444, 7445, but those only marked for identification, pending translation. And then 7446 and 7447, that was the document -- we ruled on that after considering your objection. Now we want to have the document numbers for these four documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7444 shall be assigned Exhibit P2442, marked for identification, pending translation. 65 ter document 7445 shall be assigned Exhibit P2443, marked for identification, pending translation. 65 ter document 7446 shall be assigned Exhibit P2444. And 65 ter document 7447 shall be assigned Exhibit P2445. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise for my mistake I made in mixing up the two intercepts or conversations. Now our problems seem to be resolved. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to seek clarification with regard to P2244. We know that there is a translation into Serbian. The document was originally drafted in French. There is no translation into English. The Defence doesn't mind that fact. However, we would like to see whether the Prosecution has any problems with that, whether we may receive an English translation in the meantime, and that would help us a lot. As regards documents in French, if they are translated into Serbian, they don't need to have English translations, as far as we are concerned. As far as the other participants in the proceedings are concerned, they should state their opinion with this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, especially for those who are not able to read French fluently, it would be very helpful. On the other hand, I was told earlier that our Translation Unit doesn't translate documents -- French documents into English, and the other way around. But if it is -- if we could get an English translation, it would be very helpful. We would --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand we've actually made a request to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we need our second break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have our second break and resume 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could go to the next tab. It should be tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, Mr. Janc, 65 ter 5542. What we should have here is an intercept from the Croatian authorities from 10 September 1994. We're having problems with the B/C/S version of it. That's no problem. I can read some of it into the record until that comes up. All right, we have something. Great. Mr. Janc, have you seen this intercept before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And just in general terms, were you able to find information from other sources that corroborate the contents of this intercept? Once again, it's 10 September 1994. It's timed at 10 hours 33 minutes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms, I would say yes, because there is no documents which would say exactly what we can see here in this intercept, but there are UNPROFOR documents which are talking about the tensions in this Bihac pocket on this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're referring to the part of the conversation that, well, indicated here that a message was sent to General Tolimir regarding the shelling of the town of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what documents were you able to identify? You mentioned that there were some UN documents.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, there are actually two documents, one of which is in French, which I couldn't understand it, and was the relevant portion which was marked -- was read out to me because I don't speak French, and the other one is in English. The French document is from 10 September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at that one.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: The English one is from the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll take a look at the French one, which is 65 ter 7448. Mr. President, this one is also a document that needs to be added -- or I would be moving to add to the 65 ter list of the Prosecution. I don't believe we have a B/C/S translation of this document either. For the benefit of General Tolimir, this is a document to Mr. Annan from Mr. De Lapresle of UNPROFOR Zagreb, dated 10 September 1994, and it talks about the situation in the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is this the document that you're referring to, Mr. Janc, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated that part of this -- what's recounted in this document is reflected -- or, rather, reflects on the content of the intercept which was 65 ter 5542; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. On page 4 of this document, there is a first paragraph which is talking about the situation in Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at that. That's item 12 on page 4, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I could take a stab at reading this, although somewhat reluctantly, in order to have it translated into the record, but could you tell us, generally, what you refer to in this paragraph that's relevant -- of relevance, rather, to the intercept in question?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. As I explained, I can't say exactly what's written there because I don't read French. But as I was read out this paragraph, I could establish that this was somehow connected to the general situation in Bihac pocket at that time which -- where there were tensions between VRS and the other side in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the first couple of sentences of this document, which I think might help General Tolimir a little bit, and I'll do my best to read it into the record so it can be translated for everyone. It says, at item 12 [French spoken]. [Interpretation] "... return to Zagreb, I was able to have an update --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are technical problems via receiving English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I thought it was my speech, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I don't think that it was as bad as you suppose. Now we receive French translation on the English channel. You should try once more, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll try again. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At paragraph 12, it reads -- [French spoken]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Regrettably, we don't receive any English translation on the English channel. Your French is too good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Evidently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you receive a B/C/S translation, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian interpretation is functioning, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's hard work for you, it's really a challenge. We have it -- oh, yes. You should just continue, and we'll see if it will work.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It will work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It continues: [Interpretation] "As I returned to Zagreb, I was in a position to take stock of the situation by phone with General Rose in order to co-ordinate the organisation of meetings between the various parties and look for a settlement of this Bihac problem. He told me about his close contacts with the Pale and Sarajevo authorities. And regarding these contacts, he said he had asked Mr. Ganic to have the mortar fire stopped immediately, mortar fire that had taken place at 12.00 noon today, by the Bosnian forces from the Bihac Villa as a response to the fire from the Serb Bosnian forces against military objectives located close to that town. A similar action was taken with General Tolimir in Pale, with the aim of having any Serbian provocation stopped, as I requested already yesterday, in the evening, in my letter to General Mladic." [In English] Is this the relevant part of the document you considered in relation to the intercept in question, which talks about the shelling of the town of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And let me show you the other document that you referred to, which is 65 ter 7449.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish to draw attention to page 70, line 3. In the English text, it says "a similar action." I think it would be better to say "a similar demarche" or "an analogous demarche."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is a more literal quotation. Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I've asked for 64 [sic] 7449 in e-court, I would just like to show that to Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have another document, and again without a translation. This one, for the benefit of General Tolimir, is also dated 10 September 1994, and this one is from Akashi to Annan, and it is also concerning the situation in Bihac. In particular, in -- first of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you consider this document also in relation to the intercept that we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what about this document bears on the content of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Again, as the one before, we will see on page 2 of this document that it is talking about the situation in Bihac, the second paragraph and the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there anything in particular in this paragraph that you found supported the intercept -- supported at least the reliability of the content of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. The intercept, itself, says that a message was sent to General Tolimir saying that aerial attacks by NATO forces on Serbian units would follow unless the shelling of the town of Bihac did not stop as a matter of urgency. And here in the second paragraph, we can see the last part of the paragraph written that: "Accordingly, General Rose has advised the BSA of our assessment of the situation and warned them not to attack the safe area." So this is the sentence which I would say correspond to the intercept, although we can see here in the document, itself, that it refers to General Rose. On the other hand, on -- in intercept we have General Stanley who is calling or sending message to General Tolimir. But I would say that this does not change the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I would like to tender these documents; that is, the intercept as well as the corroborating material. That's 65 ter 7448 and 7449. Neither has an English translation, and I believe we've submitted translation requests for them into B/C/S, and also, for the French document, I believe, also into English, as well as the intercept, itself, which is 65 ter 5542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir if there is any objection to add document 65 ter 7448 and 7449 to the 65 ter exhibit list and any objection to the admission of these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do have an objection. These documents are not correct and are not authentic. May it be checked whether General Stanley was ever at the UNPROFOR Command? There's something wrong here. This is a forgery. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please indicate to which document you are referring?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 05542, the first sentence, where it says "General M. Stanley." I have never heard of General Stanley. I'm not supposed to testify, but maybe Mr. Vanderpuye would be able to clarify with the witness whether a General Stanley was in Bosnia during the conflict, whether he was affiliated with the UNPROFOR Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I suppose I can ask Mr. Tolimir -- Mr. Janc whether or not he can shed light on this, if you're able to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at this point. I would need to take a closer look into this name to find out. So right now, I can't say, but deeply inside, I think I heard this name. But I can't confirm for the fact right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see an indication in the intercept, 5542, of where General Stanley is at the time that this message is sent?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: No, we don't know where he was at the time. It might be Sarajevo, it might be also Zagreb or anywhere else, so we don't see that from the intercept, itself, where is he calling from and where is he from, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I would still tender these documents. I don't see that the fact that General Tolimir doesn't know or -- well, he's not testifying - has represented that he doesn't know who General Stanley is, or the fact that General Stanley is not -- his affiliation isn't indicated in the intercept has any bearing on whether or not the communication was actually made, as indicated in the intercept, particularly to the extent that what is indicated in the intercept relates to events which are otherwise fully corroborated by independent means. Specifically, it refers to -- it refers to a warning to the Serb forces concerning the shelling of the town of Bihac, which we can see is reflected in the two UN documents that we've just reviewed, one which is a specific warning, which is under 65 ter 7449, on the second page of that, which Mr. Janc just testified about, concerning a warning to the BSA not to attack the safe area of Bihac, in particular, and that the force commander has also sent a letter to General Mladic concerning this, and then also, in the version -- not the -- rather, not the version, the other document, which is 65 ter 7448 from Mr. De Lapresle, the one that we've just read in French, indicating that Dr. Ganic was asked to cease immediately firing mortars as of 1200 hours on the part of the Bosnian side from Bihac in response to firing from the Serb side, which was referred to as against military objectives in the proximity of the town. And this is, on its face, reflected in the substance of the intercept, 65 ter 5542. And so I think on that basis alone, it satisfies the admissibility criteria under Rule 89, notwithstanding General Tolimir's objective [sic] that he doesn't know who General Stanley is or what his affiliation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have two questions, one for the Defence and the other one for the Prosecution. General Tolimir, you challenge both documents. What is your basis, apart from the fact that General Stanley, according to you, was not present in Sarajevo at the moment of the facts? That's my question for the Defence. In other words, do you also challenge the substance of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua, I do not challenge the substance of the document. It suits me to have it admitted because it's false. I don't know any general by this name. And I would be very happy were this document admitted into evidence because then I could prove that these documents are spurious and unreliable. So we, the Defence, have nothing against this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now my question for the Prosecution: Could you tell us where those two documents come from? What is their source?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The two documents, Your Honour, are UN documents. We can see that one is from the force commander of UNPROFOR from Zagreb, and the other one is from Yasushi Akashi from UNPROFOR in Zagreb as well. Both of them are UN documents, and they are -- well, they were provided to us by the UN for the purposes of use before the Tribunal. The other one is -- rather, not the other one. The intercept, itself, as we know, is of Croatian origin, from prior evidence in the case. If you'd like me to elaborate on it, I can, but I think we'd have to go into private session for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this explanation. It's not necessary to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just a clarification. Your last comment was that you don't have anything against admission of this document, but you challenge the content of it and the way it was produced, this intercept. And, therefore, is it your position that you will deal with that during the cross-examination of this witness, or with another witness, or during the Defence case? Everything is possible. Is my understanding correct that you do not object to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not objecting to anything. I just want to tell the Chamber that there are incorrect things in this document and it's misleading for the Chamber. If there's a general mentioned in the document, we have to know who the general is. There aren't all that many generals. And it says here that there's a general in Zagreb and one in Sarajevo, so the transcript does not reflect the documents. Is the transcript to be trusted or not? Is it incorrect, imprecise, unclear? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First, since there is no objection by Mr. Tolimir to the admission of the intercept, which is 65 ter 5542, it will be received, with your remarks, Mr. Tolimir, you have put on the record in relation to a certain General Stanley and with your remark that, in your opinion, it is a forgery. This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 5542 shall be assigned Exhibit P2446. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The other two documents will be marked for identification, pending translation. And, again, we hope that it will be possible to receive an English translation of the French letter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7448 shall be assigned Exhibit P2447, marked for identification, pending translation. And 65 ter document 7449 shall be assigned Exhibit P2448, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could show the witness, please, 65 ter 5408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that we are now dealing with documents behind tab 4 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the English, let me ask you, Mr. Janc: Have you had a chance to review this particular intercept? It's dated October 5, 1994, and timed at 1500 hours 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to identify any additional documents supporting the reliability of the content of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There are two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what those were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. One is an intercept again from Sarajevo State Security Service, from this same date. And in my opinion, it is about the same conversation. And the second one is a document -- is a UN document again, UNPROFOR document, a daily report from that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So in this particular intercept, we can see that it refers to the Main Staff having dispatched General Tolimir to Kopaci village, and then in parenthesis it says "(Gorazde)," "... to co-ordinate with the UNPROFOR the evacuation part of the population from Gorazde." If I could, I'd like to show you 65 ter 5611. And this document, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is the intercept I was talking about before. MUP SDB, State Security Service, from 5th of October, 1994. It's a conversation -- transcribed conversation of the intercept communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in particular, what part of this conversation is reflected in the intercept 65 ter 5408 that we've just looked at, the Croatian origin -- the intercept from Croatian origins?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. If you move down into this, we can see the paragraph one before the last one, which starts with "M." And this is General Milovanovic saying: "I will send General Tolimir and his crew to Kopaci near Gorazde to co-ordinate the evacuation process with UNPROFOR and the Muslims." So it's talking about the evacuation and General Tolimir being dispatched to Kopaci village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you find that this intercept, that is the MUP intercept, Sarajevo SDB sector, supported or corroborated the Croatian-origin intercept in other ways, or in any other way, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, also there are some other parts which are talking about the issue of how many vehicles have been approved for evacuation, and there is a dispute regarding the UNHCR vehicle in both intercepts. So it's -- actually, in this intercept we have more information than we have in a summary of Croatian intercepts, but everything what is in Croatian intercept is also in this one, in BiH one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at one last document, if we could, Mr. President, and then we can wind up for the day, and that is 65 ter 7452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before this document is tendered, it might be a good idea if the Prosecutor were to clarify with the witness why this is a translation from English. If this is an intercept, was it the service that intercepted the conversation that translated it as well? And if not, who did translate it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It seems to be a quite similar issue we dealt with earlier with another document. In the document 65 ter 5611, we see the heading "Report Submitted on 5th of October, 1994, Translated from English." I take it that Mr. Tolimir is referring to that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm certain that he is. If we look under item number 1, we can see that there is a clear indication that the conversation was again mediated through an interpreter, and it seems that the same explanation that obtained with respect to the other intercept from the MUP Sarajevo SDB Sector would apply in this circumstance as well, as well as the same arguments with respect to its admissibility and provenance in respect of the intercept of Croatian origin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the arguments are put on the record, as with the previous document. Please carry on and try to come to an end for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We should have, hopefully, 65 ter -- no, we don't. 65 ter 7452 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And is this a document that you considered, in terms of evaluating the reliability of the intercept that we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. This is a daily sitrep from 5th of October, 1994, and the relevant part is on page, I think, 8 of this document, paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's just go straight there and take a look at that. Tell us what about this particular paragraph supports the reliability of the intercept in question, 65 ter 5408.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: First, before paragraph 32, we can see "UNMO team Gorazde," and here is the summary for Gorazde, what was happening. And paragraph 33 is talking about the humanitarian activity, and we can see that: "Today UNPROFOR escorted and transported out of the pocket: 33 Serbs to Kopaci at 1530 ..." And so on and so on. And the last paragraph, it says: "The operation went well, and General Tolimir (head of security) was present." So this paragraph corroborates the intercept, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Janc. Mr. President, I see we're out of time, so I guess we'll -- I'll tender these tomorrow so that we can cut it short now, and we'll pick up then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a very good proposal. It is appreciated. We deal with that tomorrow. And we will resume tomorrow, in the afternoon, at 2.15 in the same Courtroom III. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of July, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
